paragraphs: Learning goal: Explore how authors and illustrators build characters, places and events.
Useful words: A character is a person, animal or other being in a story. Setting means where and when. An event is something that happens. An author writes; an illustrator makes the pictures.
Learning goal: Help children share a thoughtful response to a story or poem.
Useful words: A response is what we think, feel or say about a text. A connection links a text detail with our own experience. A memory is something we remember.
Learning goal: Discuss who is in a story, where and when it happens, and how its events fit together.

How to use this guide: Read a whole story, model one focus, try it together and ask for the clue. These six learning focuses match Practice A–F in the worksheet pack; choose the section the child needs rather than completing everything at once.
I can: name characters and the place/time; follow connected events; explain an idea with a story clue; compare story features and discuss them with someone.

Useful words: Character: a person, animal or other story participant. Setting: where and when events happen. Plot: the connected events of a story. Problem: what goes wrong. Solution: how it is resolved.
Learning goal: Listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, then imitate and invent their sound patterns.

How to use this guide: Listen to a whole text, echo a model, make an original change and discuss its sound. These six learning focuses match Practice A–F in the worksheet pack. Sound words, repetition and performance support the central work of hearing, imitating and inventing alliteration and rhyme.
I can: hear matching beginning and ending sounds; echo a pattern; invent a meaningful new version; perform or communicate it and discuss what I notice.

Useful words: Alliteration: nearby words repeating a beginning sound. Rhyme: words with matching ending sounds. Repetition: a word or line heard again. Sound word: a word that suggests a sound. Performance: how we say, sing or communicate a text.
Learning goal: I can orally retell or adapt a familiar story using its characters, important events, story language and structure.

Start together: Read or hear a whole story several times. Make it familiar before asking the child to retell it. Read the short Sam and Jo story below together first, then revisit it across the focuses.
Useful words: Retell: tell a story again. Adapt: change part of a story. Character: who is in a story. Setting: where and when it happens. First, next, then, last help tell the order.
Learning goal: I can discuss different texts and explain their jobs using clues in the words, pictures and layout.
Start together: Read the short messages aloud together. Compare their jobs and point to clues. Use school, home and community examples; decoding and handwriting are not this code’s target.

Useful words: Text: a message made with words, pictures or both. Purpose: the text’s job. Feature: a part we can notice, such as a heading, picture or step. Clue: something that helps us work out the job.
Learning goal: I can take turns, communicate clearly, show understanding and build a conversation with ideas and questions.
Start together: Use one focus at a time. Model a short exchange, practise with a classmate or adult, then reduce help. Try both everyday talk and a planned group discussion.
Useful words: Topic: what we talk about. Turn: time to share a message. Listen: try to understand. Reply: respond to a message. Question: ask for information.
Learn with short examples

These six teaching focuses help you compare imaginative, informative and persuasive texts. They are teaching sections within one curriculum code. An adult can read the short texts aloud while you concentrate on their meaning.
